claim: Drosophila wing size is regulated by JNK signaling during development.
source: Here we show that Drosophila wing size is regulated by JNK signaling during development.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: JNK is active in a stripe along the center of developing wings.
source: JNK is active in a stripe along the center of developing wings
evidence: Supported by pJNK antibody staining shown in Figure 1B-C and described in the text.

claim: Modulating JNK signaling within the pJNK stripe changes organ size.
source: modulating JNK signaling within this stripe changes organ size
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing that inhibition or activation of JNK in the ptc domain affects wing size (Figures 2A-L).

claim: The JNK stripe influences proliferation in a non-canonical, Jun-independent manner by inhibiting the Hippo pathway.
source: This JNK stripe influences proliferation in a non-canonical, Jun-independent manner by inhibiting the Hippo pathway.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing that jun knockdown does not affect wing size (Figure 3A-B) while jub and yki manipulations do (Figure 3C-P).

claim: Localized JNK activity is established by Hedgehog signaling, where Ci elevates dTRAF1 expression.
source: Localized JNK activity is established by Hedgehog signaling, where Ci elevates dTRAF1 expression.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing that Ci knockdown eliminates pJNK (Figure 4A-B) and that dTRAF1 is upregulated in ptc cells (Figure 5C).

claim: The dTRAF1 homolog, TRAF4, is amplified in numerous cancers.
source: As the dTRAF1 homolog, TRAF4, is amplified in numerous cancers
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and discussion with citation support.

claim: These findings provide a new mechanism for how the Hedgehog pathway could contribute to tumorigenesis.
source: these findings provide a new mechanism for how the Hedgehog pathway could contribute to tumorigenesis
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings connecting Hh signaling to JNK activation and cancer.

claim: Modulation of JNK signaling centers in developing antennae and legs changes their sizes.
source: Finally, modulation of JNK signaling centers in developing antennae and legs changes their sizes
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 6 where JNK inhibition or activation in antenna and leg discs affects their size.

claim: JNK has a more generalizable role in developmental organ size control.
source: suggesting a more generalizable role for JNK signaling in developmental organ size control
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that JNK affects size in multiple organs (wing, antenna, leg).

claim: Two independently generated antibodies that recognize phosphorylated, active JNK specifically label a stripe in the pouch of developing wildtype third instar wing discs.
source: Two independently generated antibodies that recognize the phosphorylated, active form of JNK (pJNK) specifically label a stripe in the pouch of developing wildtype third instar wing discs (Figure 1B–C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: Directly stated and shown in Figure 1B-C and supplementary figures.

claim: Localized pJNK staining is not detected in hemizygous JNKK mutant discs.
source: Importantly, localized pJNK staining is not detected in hemizygous JNKK mutant discs (Figure 1D–E; hepr75/Y)
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D-E with genetic mutant analysis.

claim: pJNK staining is lost in clones of JNKK mutant cells within the stripe.
source: in clones of JNKK mutant cells within the stripe (Figure 1F; hepr75, FRT10/Ubi-GFP, FRT10;; MKRS, hs-FLP/+)
evidence: Demonstrated by clonal analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: pJNK staining is lost following over-expression of the JNK phosphatase puckered.
source: following over-expression of the JNK phosphatase puckered (puc) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I; ap-Gal4, UAS-puc)
evidence: Shown in supplementary figure with genetic manipulation.

claim: pJNK staining is lost following RNAi-mediated knockdown of bsk using two independent RNAi lines.
source: following RNAi-mediated knockdown of bsk using two independent, functionally validated RNAi lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K–L; rn-Gal4, UAS-bskRNAi#1 or ptc-Gal4, UAS-bskRNAi#2; see Experimental Genotypes for full genotypes and conditions) (Glise et al., 1995; MacDonald et al., 2013; Martín-Blanco et al., 1998; Pérez-Garijo et al., 2013; Weber et al., 2000; Xu and Rubin, 1993).
evidence: Demonstrated with RNAi experiments shown in supplementary figures and supported by citations.

claim: The stripe of localized pJNK staining is adjacent to the anterior-posterior compartment boundary.
source: The stripe of localized pJNK staining appeared to be adjacent to the anterior-posterior (A/P) compartment boundary, a location known to play a key role in organizing wing growth, and a site of active Hedgehog (Hh) signaling (Basler and Struhl, 1994; Tabata and Kornberg, 1994; Zecca et al., 1995).
evidence: Stated in the text with citation support for the role of the A/P boundary.

claim: pJNK co-localizes with the Hh target gene patched (ptc).
source: Indeed, pJNK co-localizes with the Hh target gene patched (ptc) (Figure 1G; ptc-Gal4, UAS-RFP).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1G with co-localization imaging.

claim: Expression of the JNK phosphatase puc in ptc cells specifically abrogates pJNK staining.
source: Expression of the JNK phosphatase puc in these cells specifically abrogated pJNK staining (Figure 1H; ptc-Gal4, UAS-puc)
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1H with genetic manipulation.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of bsk in ptc cells abrogates pJNK staining.
source: as did RNAi-mediated knockdown of bsk (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1L; ptc-Gal4, UAS-bskRNA#i1or2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1I and supplementary figure.

claim: At earlier developmental stages pJNK staining is detected in all wing pouch cells.
source: Indeed, while at earlier developmental stages pJNK staining is detected in all wing pouch cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)

claim: The presence of a localized stripe of pJNK correlates with the time when the majority of wing disc growth occurs.
source: the presence of a localized stripe of pJNK correlates with the time when the majority of wing disc growth occurs (1000 cells/disc at mid-L3 stage to 50,000 cells/disc at 20 hr after pupation, (Garcia-Bellido, 2009)
evidence: Stated with citation to support the timing of wing disc growth.

claim: Inhibition of JNK signaling in the posterior compartment previously led to the conclusion that JNK does not play a role in wing development.
source: Inhibition of JNK signaling in the posterior compartment previously led to the conclusion that JNK does not play a role in wing development (McEwen and Peifer, 2005).
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: Inhibition of JNK in all wing blade cells or specifically in ptc-expressing cells results in smaller adult wings.
source: Inhibition of JNK in all wing blade cells (rotund-Gal4, rn-Gal4) or specifically in ptc-expressing cells (ptc-Gal4) resulted in smaller adult wings in all cases, up to 40% reduced in the strongest cases (Figures 2A–F, 2J–K, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by multiple genetic manipulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Expression of a control transgene (UAS-GFP) does not affect wing size.
source: Importantly, expression of a control transgene (UAS-GFP) did not affect wing size (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C; ptc-Gal4, UAS-GFP).
evidence: Control experiment shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Hypomorphic hepr75/Y animals have smaller wing discs.
source: Nevertheless, hypomorphic hepr75/Y animals, while pupal lethal, also have smaller wing discs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: Shown in supplementary figure with mutant analysis.

claim: Animals with reduced JNK signaling due to bskDN expression have smaller wing discs.
source: as do animals with reduced JNK signaling due to bskDN expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–I; ap-Gal4, UAS-bskDN).

claim: Total body size is not affected by inhibiting JNK in the wing.
source: Importantly, total body size is not affected by inhibiting JNK in the wing. Even for the smallest wings generated (rn-Gal4, UAS-bskDN), total animal body size is not altered (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,E).
evidence: Demonstrated in supplementary figure showing body length measurements.

claim: Expression of eiger in the ptc domain causes a dramatic increase in wing disc size without apparent duplications or changes in disc shape.
source: Despite induction of cell death as previously reported (Igaki et al., 2002) and late larval lethality, we observed a dramatic increase in wing disc size without apparent duplications or changes in the shape of the disc (Figures 2H–I and 2L; ptc-Gal4, UAS-egr).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2H-I and 2L with citation to prior work on eiger.

claim: Wing discs with elevated JNK signaling are larger than controls assayed at the same time point.
source: While changes in organ size could be due to changing developmental time, wing discs with elevated JNK signaling were already larger than controls assayed at the same time point (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C; ptc-Gal4 and ptc-Gal4, UAS-egr).
evidence: Demonstrated in supplementary figure with time-matched controls.

claim: Inhibition of JNK does not shorten developmental time.
source: Similarly, inhibition of JNK did not shorten developmental time (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F; rn-Gal4, UAS-bskDN).

claim: Expression of the pro-apoptotic gene hid causes a decrease in wing size.
source: Finally, the observed increase in organ size is not due to induction of apoptosis, as expression of the pro-apoptotic gene hid does not increase organ size (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–F). In contrast, it causes a decrease in wing size (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–F).

claim: Co-expression of diap1 or p35 does not significantly affect the growth effect of egr expression.
source: Furthermore, co-expression of diap1 or p35 did not significantly affect the growth effect of egr expression (p>0.05; Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 2H–I; ptc-Gal4, UAS-egr, UAS-diap1 and ptc-Gal4, UAS-egr, UAS-p35)
evidence: Shown in Figure 2L and supplementary figures with statistical analysis.

claim: The growth effect of egr expression is dependent on Bsk activity.
source: while the effect was dependent on Bsk activity (p<0.05; Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 2G; ptc-Gal4, UAS-egr, UAS-bskDN).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2L and supplementary figure with statistical analysis.

claim: No obvious defects in wing venation pattern are observed following JNK inhibition.
source: In stark contrast to known developmental morphogens, we did not observe any obvious defects in wing venation pattern following JNK inhibition (Figure 2A–B)

claim: Even a slight reduction in Dpp signaling results in dramatic wing vein patterning defects.
source: Indeed, even a slight reduction in Dpp signaling results in dramatic wing vein patterning defects (Figure 2—figure supplement 3K).

claim: Inhibiting Dpp signaling causes a reduction in wing size along the A-P axis, while JNK inhibition causes a global reduction.
source: Second, inhibiting Dpp signaling causes a reduction in wing size along the A-P axis, while JNK inhibition causes a global reduction (Figure 2—figure supplement 3J–L).
evidence: Shown in supplementary figure comparing Dpp and JNK effects.

claim: Ectopic Dpp expression increases growth in the form of duplicated structures.
source: Furthermore, ectopic Dpp expression increases growth in the form of duplicated structures (Zecca et al., 1995)

claim: Increased JNK signaling results in a global increase in size without duplications.
source: while increased JNK signaling results in a global increase in size (Figure 2H–I).

claim: Reducing Dpp signaling abolishes pSMAD staining.
source: Molecularly, we confirm that reducing Dpp signaling abolishes pSMAD staining

claim: Inhibiting JNK signaling does not affect pSMAD staining.
source: while quantitative data shows that inhibiting JNK signaling does not (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D–I).
evidence: Shown in supplementary figure with quantitative analysis.

claim: Dpp is not upstream of pJNK, as reduction in Dpp signaling does not affect pJNK.
source: Furthermore, we also find that Dpp is not upstream of pJNK, as reduction in Dpp signaling does not affect pJNK (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).

claim: Inhibition of JNK does not affect EGFR signaling (pERK).
source: Finally, we found that inhibition of JNK does not affect EGFR signaling (pERK) and that inhibition of EGFR does not affect the establishment of pJNK (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C and 4A).

claim: Inhibition of EGFR does not affect the establishment of pJNK.
source: inhibition of EGFR does not affect the establishment of pJNK (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C and 4A).

claim: Wings with reduced size due to JNK inhibition do not show changes in cell size.
source: We examined wings with reduced size due to JNK inhibition and did not detect changes in cell size or apoptosis (Figure 2M–O and Figure 2—figure supplement 1L–N; rn-Gal4, UAS-bskDN)
evidence: Shown in Figure 2M-O and supplementary figures.

claim: Wings with reduced size due to JNK inhibition do not show changes in apoptosis.
source: We examined wings with reduced size due to JNK inhibition and did not detect changes in cell size or apoptosis (Figure 2M–O and Figure 2—figure supplement 1L–N; rn-Gal4, UAS-bskDN)
evidence: Shown in Figure 2M-O and supplementary figures.

claim: pJNK controls organ size by regulating cell number.
source: suggesting that pJNK controls organ size by regulating cell number.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that cell size and apoptosis are not affected.

claim: The cell death inhibitor p35 is unable to rescue the decreased size following JNK inhibition.
source: Consistently, the cell death inhibitor p35 was unable to rescue the decreased size following JNK inhibition (Figure 2G; rn-Gal4, UAS-p35, UAS-bskDN).

claim: Inhibition of JNK signaling results in a decrease in proliferation.
source: Indeed, inhibition of JNK signaling resulted in a decrease in proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J–K; ap-Gal4, UAS-bskDN)
evidence: Shown in supplementary figure with PH3 staining.

claim: Elevation of JNK signaling in the ptc domain results in an increase in cell proliferation in the enlarged wing disc.
source: while elevation of JNK signaling in the ptc domain resulted in an increase in cell proliferation in the enlarged wing disc (Figure 2P–T; ptc-Gal4, UAS-egr).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2P-T with EdU staining.

claim: Increased proliferation following JNK elevation is not restricted to the ptc domain.
source: Importantly, this increased proliferation is not restricted to the ptc domain, consistent with previous reports that JNK can promote proliferation non-autonomously (Enomoto and Igaki, 2012; Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008; Ryoo et al., 2004; Sun and Irvine, 2011; Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated with citation support for non-autonomous JNK effects.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of jun in ptc cells does not change wing size.
source: Interestingly, RNAi-mediated knockdown of jun in ptc cells does not change wing size (Figure 3A–B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F; ptc-Gal4, UAS-junRNAi#1or2; Both RNAi lines can effectively inhibit jun activity, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B)
evidence: Shown in Figure 3A-B and supplementary figures.

claim: Analysis of jun mutant clones in the wing disc shows no effect on wing size.
source: which is consistent with previous analysis of jun mutant clones in the wing disc (Kockel et al., 1997).

claim: A reporter of canonical JNK signaling downstream of jun (puc-lacZ) is not expressed in the pJNK stripe.
source: Furthermore, in agreement with this, a reporter of canonical JNK signaling downstream of jun (puc-lacZ [Ring and Martinez Arias, 1993]) is not expressed in the pJNK stripe (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Shown in supplementary figure with citation.

claim: Knockdown of fos (kayak, kay) alone or with junRNAi does not affect wing size.
source: Finally, knockdown of fos (kayak, kay) alone or with junRNAi did not affect wing size (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–H; rn-Gal4, UAS-kayRNiA#1or2 and rn-Gal4, UAS-junRNAi#1, UAS-kayRNiA#1or2).

claim: Canonical JNK signaling through jun does not function in the pJNK stripe to regulate wing size.
source: Together, these data indicate that canonical JNK signaling through jun does not function in the pJNK stripe to regulate wing size.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing jun independence.

claim: JNK signaling regulates the Hippo pathway to induce autonomous and non-autonomous proliferation during tumorigenesis and regeneration via activation of Yorkie.
source: JNK signaling regulates the Hippo pathway to induce autonomous and non-autonomous proliferation during tumorigenesis and regeneration via activation of the transcriptional regulator Yorkie (Yki) (Bakal et al., 2008; Enomoto and Igaki, 2012; Sun and Irvine, 2011).

claim: JNK activates Yki via direct phosphorylation of Jub.
source: Recently it has been shown that JNK activates Yki via direct phosphorylation of Jub (Sun and Irvine, 2013).

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of jub in the ptc stripe results in adults with smaller wings.
source: To test whether this link between JNK and Jub could account for the role of localized pJNK in organ size control during development, we performed RNAi-mediated knockdown of jub in the ptc stripe, and observed adults with smaller wings (Figure 3C–D; ptc-Gal4, UAS-jubRNAi#1or2).

claim: The effect of JNK loss on wing size can be partially suppressed in a heterozygous lats mutant background.
source: Indeed, the effect of JNK loss on wing size can be partially suppressed in a heterozygous lats mutant background (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D; rn-Gal4, UAS-bskDN, latse26-1/+)

claim: Increasing downstream yki expression in all wing cells can rescue wing size following JNK inhibition.
source: and increasing downstream yki expression in all wing cells (Figure 3E–F; rn-Gal4, UAS-yki, UAS-bskDN) or just within the ptc domain (Figure 3G–H; ptc-Gal4, UAS-yki, UAS-bskDN) can rescue wing size following JNK inhibition.

claim: Increasing downstream yki expression within the ptc domain can rescue wing size following JNK inhibition.
source: or just within the ptc domain (Figure 3G–H; ptc-Gal4, UAS-yki, UAS-bskDN) can rescue wing size following JNK inhibition.

claim: pJNK controls Yki activity autonomously within the ptc stripe, leading to a global change in cell proliferation.
source: These results suggest that pJNK controls Yki activity autonomously within the ptc stripe, leading to a global change in cell proliferation.
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiments and proliferation data.

claim: Inhibition of JNK in the ptc stripe translates to homogeneous changes in anterior and posterior wing growth.
source: Consistently, inhibition of JNK in the ptc stripe translates to homogeneous changes in anterior and posterior wing growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B).

claim: Overexpression or inhibition of Yki signaling in the ptc stripe results in a global change in wing size.
source: Similarly, overexpression or inhibition of Yki signaling in the ptc stripe also results in a global change in wing size (Figure 3I–L and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B; ptc-Gal4, UAS-yki; ptc-Gal4, UAS-ykiRNAi).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3I-L and supplementary figures.

claim: Expression of activated Yki in the ptc stripe causes very large tumors and lethality.
source: Expression of this activated Yki in the ptc stripe caused very large tumors and lethality (data not shown).

claim: Inhibiting JNK in the context of activated Yki expression does not affect tumor formation or lethality.
source: Importantly, inhibiting JNK in this context did not affect the formation of these tumors or the lethality (data not shown; ptc-Gal4, UAS-ykiS111A,S168A,S250A.V5, UAS-bskDN).

claim: Inhibiting both JNK and Yki together does not enhance the phenotype of Yki inhibition alone.
source: Furthermore, inhibiting both JNK and Yki together does not enhance the phenotype of Yki inhibition alone (Figure 3M–N and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–F; ptc-Gal4, UAS-ykiRNAi, UAS-bskDN and ptc-Gal4, UAS-ykiRNAi, UAS-puc)
evidence: Shown in Figure 3M-N and supplementary figures.

claim: Yki is epistatic to JNK, instead of acting in parallel processes.
source: further supporting the idea that Yki is epistatic to JNK, instead of acting in parallel processes.

claim: Mutants of the Yki downstream target four-jointed (fj) have small wings with normal patterning.
source: Mutants of the Yki downstream target four-jointed (fj) have small wings with normal patterning, and fj is known to propagate Hippo signaling and affect proliferation non-autonomously (Ambegaonkar et al., 2012; Harvey and Tapon, 2007; Strutt et al., 2004; Villano and Katz, 1995; Willecke et al., 2008).

claim: fj is known to propagate Hippo signaling and affect proliferation non-autonomously.
source: and fj is known to propagate Hippo signaling and affect proliferation non-autonomously (Ambegaonkar et al., 2012; Harvey and Tapon, 2007; Strutt et al., 2004; Villano and Katz, 1995; Willecke et al., 2008).

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of fj in ptc cells does not cause an obvious change in wing size.
source: Although RNAi-mediated knockdown of fj in ptc cells does not cause an obvious change in wing size, it is sufficient to block the Yki-induced effect on increasing wing size (Figure 3O–P and Figure 3—figure supplement 2G–H; ptc-Gal4, UAS-yki, UAS-fjRNAiand ptc-Gal4, UAS-fjRNAi).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3O-P and supplementary figures.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of fj is sufficient to block the Yki-induced effect on increasing wing size.
source: it is sufficient to block the Yki-induced effect on increasing wing size (Figure 3O–P and Figure 3—figure supplement 2G–H; ptc-Gal4, UAS-yki, UAS-fjRNAiand ptc-Gal4, UAS-fjRNAi).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3O-P and supplementary figures.

claim: Overexpression of fj reduces wing size.
source: However, overexpression of fj also reduces wing size, which makes it not possible to test for a simple epistatic relationship (ptc-Gal4, UAS-fj; Figure 3—figure supplement 2I–J).

claim: Localized pJNK regulates wing size not by Jun-dependent canonical JNK signaling, but rather by Jun-independent non-canonical JNK signaling involving the Hippo pathway.
source: Overall, these data are consistent with the notion that localized pJNK regulates wing size not by Jun-dependent canonical JNK signaling, but rather by Jun-independent non-canonical JNK signaling involving the Hippo pathway.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing jun independence and Hippo pathway involvement.

claim: pJNK staining is coincident with ptc expression.
source: pJNK staining is coincident with ptc expression (Figure 1G), suggesting it could be established by Hh signaling.

claim: During development, posterior Hh protein travels across the A/P boundary, leading to activation of Ci in the stripe of anterior cells.
source: During development, posterior Hh protein travels across the A/P boundary, leading to activation of the transcription factor Cubitus interruptus (Ci) in the stripe of anterior cells (Domínguez et al., 1996; Schwartz et al., 1995).

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of ci eliminates the pJNK stripe.
source: To test whether localized activation of JNK is a consequence of Hh signaling through Ci, we performed RNAi-mediated knockdown of ci and found that the pJNK stripe is eliminated (Figure 4A–B; ptc-Gal4, UAS-ciRNAi#1or2).

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of ci results in globally reduced adult wing size.
source: Consistently, adult wing size is globally reduced (Figures 4D and 4G).

claim: A change in pJNK stripe staining is not observed following RNAi-mediated knockdown of dpp or EGFR.
source: In contrast, we do not observe a change in pJNK stripe staining following RNAi-mediated knockdown of dpp or EGFR (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–B).

claim: Expression of non-processable Ci leads to increased Hh signaling.
source: Expression of non-processable Ci leads to increased Hh signaling (Price and Kalderon, 1999).

claim: Expression of active Ci in ptc cells leads to an increase in pJNK signal and larger, well-patterned adult wings.
source: Expression of this active Ci in ptc cells leads to an increase in pJNK signal and larger, well-patterned adult wings (Figures 4C,E, and 4G; ptc-Gal4, UAS-CiACT).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4C, E, and G.

claim: Inhibition of JNK in wings expressing active Ci blocks Ci's effects, and resulting wings are similar in size to JNK inhibition alone.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of JNK in wings expressing active Ci blocks Ci's effects, and resulting wings are similar in size to JNK inhibition alone (Figure 4F–G; ptc-Gal4, UAS-CiACT, UAS-bskDN).

claim: Hh signaling through Ci is responsible for establishing the pJNK stripe.
source: Together, these data indicate that Hh signaling through Ci is responsible for establishing the pJNK stripe.

claim: Of the total 12,676 unique genes represented on the microarray, 50.4% (6,397) are expressed in ptc domain cells, posterior cells, or both.
source: Of the total 12,676 unique genes represented on the microarray, 50.4% (6,397) are expressed in ptc domain cells, posterior cells, or both (log2 normalized expression ≥6.5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D; Supplementary file 1; Materials and methods).
evidence: Stated with reference to supplementary data and methods.

claim: 5.7% (363) of expressed genes are upregulated in ptc cells and 3.8% (242) are downregulated.
source: We thresholded on a false discovery rate <0.01 and fold change ≥1.5 and found that 5.7% (363) of expressed genes were upregulated in ptc cells and 3.8% (242) were downregulated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D; Supplementary file 2; Materials and methods).
evidence: Stated with reference to supplementary data and methods.

claim: Hh pathway genes known to be differentially expressed are identified in the microarray analysis.
source: Hh pathway genes known to be differentially expressed are identified (Figure 5B).

claim: dTRAF1 expression is more than five-fold increased in ptc cells.
source: We next asked whether any JNK pathway genes are differentially expressed and found that dTRAF1 expression is more than five-fold increased in ptc cells (Figure 5C)
evidence: Shown in Figure 5C from microarray data.

claim: Other JNK pathway members are not differentially expressed in ptc cells.
source: while other JNK pathway members are not differentially expressed (Figure 5C; Supplementary file 1; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5C and supplementary files.

claim: dTRAF1 is expressed along the A/P boundary.
source: dTRAF1 is expressed along the A/P boundary (Preiss et al., 2001)

claim: Ectopic expression of dTRAF1 activates JNK signaling.
source: and ectopic expression of dTRAF1 activates JNK signaling (Cha et al., 2003).

claim: Ci binding motifs are identified in the dTRAF1 gene.
source: Indeed, we identified Ci binding motifs in the dTRAF1 gene (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H)

claim: A previous large-scale ChIP study confirms a Ci binding site within the dTRAF1 gene.
source: and a previous large-scale ChIP study confirms a Ci binding site within the dTRAF1 gene (Chr2L: 4367100- 4371393; [Biehs et al., 2010]).

claim: A reduction in Ci leads to a 29% reduction in dTRAF1 expression in wing discs.
source: Consistently, a reduction in Ci led to a 29% reduction in dTRAF1 expression in wing discs (Figure 5J; ptc-Gal4, UAS-CiRNAi).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5J with qPCR data.

claim: Inhibition of dTRAF1 by RNAi knockdown abolishes pJNK staining.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of dTRAF1 by RNAi knockdown abolished pJNK staining (Figure 5D–E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E; ptc-Gal4, UAS-dTRAF1RNAi#1or2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5D-E and supplementary figure.

claim: Animals with dTRAF1 knockdown have smaller wings without obvious pattern defects.
source: Finally, these animals have smaller wings without obvious pattern defects (Figure 5F–I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5F-I and supplementary figures.

claim: Overexpression of dTRAF1 causes embryonic lethality.
source: Conversely, overexpression of dTRAF1 causes embryonic lethality (ptc-Gal4, UAS-dTRAF1)

claim: dTRAF1 function in the eye is Bsk-dependent.
source: Nevertheless, it has been shown that dTRAF1 function in the eye is Bsk-dependent (Cha et al., 2003).

claim: Inhibition of dTRAF1 modulates the phenotype of activated Ci signaling.
source: Finally, inhibition of dTRAF1 modulates the phenotype of activated Ci signaling (ptc-Gal4, UAS-dTRAF1RNAi, UAS-CiACT; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: The pJNK stripe in the developing wing is established by Hh signaling through Ci-mediated induction of dTRAF1 expression.
source: Together, these data reveal that the pJNK stripe in the developing wing is established by Hh signaling through Ci-mediated induction of dTRAF1 expression.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments linking Hh, Ci, dTRAF1, and pJNK.

claim: Localized centers of pJNK activity are detected during the development of eye/antenna and leg imaginal discs.
source: Finally, we detected localized centers of pJNK activity during the development of other imaginal discs including the eye/antenna and leg (Figures 6A and 6G).

claim: Inhibition of localized JNK signaling during development causes a decrease in adult antenna size.
source: Inhibition of localized JNK signaling during development caused a decrease in adult antenna size (Figures 6B–C and 6F; dll-Gal4, UAS-bskDN)

claim: Inhibition of localized JNK signaling during development causes a decrease in adult leg size.
source: and leg size (Figures 6H–I and 6L; dll-Gal4, UAS-bskDN).

claim: Increasing JNK signaling during development results in increased overall sizes of antenna and leg discs.
source: Conversely, increasing JNK signaling during development resulted in pupal lethality; nevertheless, overall sizes of antenna and leg discs were increased (Figures 6D–E and 6J–K; dll-Gal4, UAS-egr).

claim: Localized JNK signaling regulates size in organs other than the wing, suggesting a more universal effect of JNK on size control.
source: Together, these data indicate that localized JNK signaling regulates size in other organs in addition to the wing, suggesting a more universal effect of JNK on size control.
evidence: Inferred from observations in multiple organs.

claim: Classic transplantation experiments indicate that intrinsic factors within organs determine size.
source: While extrinsic factors like hormones are required for growth, classic transplantation experiments indicate that intrinsic factors within organs determine size (Bryant and Simpson, 1984).

claim: Embryonic limb buds transplanted from a large species of salamander onto a small species grow to the size characteristic of the donor.
source: For example, embryonic limb buds transplanted from a large species of salamander onto a small species grow to the size characteristic of the donor (Twitty and Schwind, 1931).

claim: Similar findings have been made in quail and chick limbs.
source: Similar findings have been made in quail and chick limbs (Iten and Murphy, 1980; Wolpert, 1978)

claim: Similar findings have been made in rat hearts and kidneys.
source: rat hearts and kidneys (Dittmer et al., 1974; Silber, 1976)

claim: Similar findings have been made in mouse thymuses.
source: and mouse thymuses (Metcalf, 1963).

claim: Developing Drosophila wings transplanted into adult abdomens grow to the proper size, indicating that the information determining size is located within the developing organ.
